items.readable_text:
Content:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the reachability relation between two vertices is defined as follows:

Content:
> A vertex [MATH: u] is reachable from a vertex [MATH: v] if there exists a directed path from [MATH: v] to [MATH: u.]

Content:
Two properties of the reachability relation for directed acyclic graphs are:

Content:
- Transitivity: if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: u,] then [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: v.]
- Antisymmetry: If [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: v] is reachable from [MATH: u] then [MATH: u = v.]

Content:
Notice that the reachability relation is transitive and symmetric (if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v], then [MATH: v] is reachable from [MATH: u]) for undirected graphs because undirected paths can be reversed.

Content:
The vertices reachable from [MATH: v] are called the successors of [MATH: v.] The set of all successors of a vertex [MATH: v] in a DAG is called the successor set of [MATH: v.] The following image highlights the successor set of vertex [MATH: v_1] along with the edges leading to those successors.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b4909a40757f029d0c22d2267b02f2c5]

Content:
Thus, the successor set of [MATH: v_1] is [MATH: \{v_2, v_4, v_5\}.]

Content:
The vertices from which it is possible to reach [MATH: u] are called the predecessors of [MATH: u.] The set of all predecessors of a vertex [MATH: u] in a DAG is called the predecessor set of [MATH: u.]

Content:
The following image highlights the predecessor set of vertex [MATH: v_5,] along with the edges leading to that set.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3fd71f1cbe3c943eaab802fa33f15648]

Content:
Thus, the predecessor set of [MATH: v_5] is [MATH: \{v_1, v_2, v_3\}.]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A vertex [MATH: u] is reachable from a vertex [MATH: v] in a directed graph if there exists a directed path starting at [MATH: v] and ending at [MATH: u.] The vertices reachable from [MATH: v] are called successors, and together, they form the successor set of [MATH: v.]

Additionally, the reachability relation is transitive: if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: u,] then [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: v.]

First, by examining the graph, we can see that [MATH: v_1] is reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

Next, the vertices [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7] are reachable from [MATH: v_1.] Hence, by transitivity, [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7] are reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

Finally, the vertex [MATH: v_3] is reachable from [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7.] Hence, by transitivity, [MATH: v_3] is reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

No other vertices can be reached. Therefore, the successor set of [MATH: v_6] is [MATH: \{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_7\}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that a cycle in a graph is a walk with no repeated vertices, except for the first and last, which are the same.

Content:
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph that contains no directed cycles.

Content:
An example of a DAG is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e53d6225a8dd55c3f1c4e26d91f63c41]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Directed Cyclic vs Directed Acyclic Graphs

Content:
The same graph that visually appears to have cycles when treated as undirected may or may not be acyclic when directed.

Content:
Among the graphs below:

Content:
- [MATH: G_1] is an undirected cyclic graph with a cycle [MATH: v_1 - v_2 - v_3 - v_4 - v_1.]
- [MATH: G_2] is a directed cyclic graph with a cycle [MATH: v_1 \to v_2 \to v_3 \to v_4 \to v_1.]
- [MATH: G_3] is a directed acyclic graph with no cycles.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/aac3e149088207ba51c7516d76cd3568]

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying a Directed Acyclic Graph

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/a82fa7195c52d8165bf640f0bb543d1d]

Which of the labeled edges in the graph above should be removed to obtain a directed acyclic graph?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a directed cycle in a directed graph is a walk with no repeated vertices, except the first and last vertex, which are the same.

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph that contains no directed cycles.

By examining our graph, we can see it contains only one cycle:
[MATH: v_2 \overset{e_3}{\to} v_5 \to v_7 \to v_4 \to v_2]

Hence, to obtain a DAG, we should break this cycle by removing one of its edges.
Of the given labeled edges, only the edge [MATH: e_3] is a part of the cycle.
Therefore, we remove [MATH: e_3.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Reachability Relation, Successors, and Predecessors

Content:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the reachability relation between two vertices is defined as follows:

Content:
> A vertex [MATH: u] is reachable from a vertex [MATH: v] if there exists a directed path from [MATH: v] to [MATH: u.]

Content:
Two properties of the reachability relation for directed acyclic graphs are:

Content:
- Transitivity: if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: u,] then [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: v.]
- Antisymmetry: If [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: v] is reachable from [MATH: u] then [MATH: u = v.]

Content:
Notice that the reachability relation is transitive and symmetric (if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v], then [MATH: v] is reachable from [MATH: u]) for undirected graphs because undirected paths can be reversed.

Content:
The vertices reachable from [MATH: v] are called the successors of [MATH: v.] The set of all successors of a vertex [MATH: v] in a DAG is called the successor set of [MATH: v.] The following image highlights the successor set of vertex [MATH: v_1] along with the edges leading to those successors.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b4909a40757f029d0c22d2267b02f2c5]

Content:
Thus, the successor set of [MATH: v_1] is [MATH: \{v_2, v_4, v_5\}.]

Content:
The vertices from which it is possible to reach [MATH: u] are called the predecessors of [MATH: u.] The set of all predecessors of a vertex [MATH: u] in a DAG is called the predecessor set of [MATH: u.]

Content:
The following image highlights the predecessor set of vertex [MATH: v_5,] along with the edges leading to that set.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3fd71f1cbe3c943eaab802fa33f15648]

Content:
Thus, the predecessor set of [MATH: v_5] is [MATH: \{v_1, v_2, v_3\}.]

---

Item 7 — Example: Identifying Reachable and Unreachable Vertices

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/d343192f6dd9194c8fee8a39e6fa8066]

Find the successor set of [MATH: v_6] in the directed acyclic graph above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A vertex [MATH: u] is reachable from a vertex [MATH: v] in a directed graph if there exists a directed path starting at [MATH: v] and ending at [MATH: u.] The vertices reachable from [MATH: v] are called successors, and together, they form the successor set of [MATH: v.]

Additionally, the reachability relation is transitive: if [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] and [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: u,] then [MATH: w] is reachable from [MATH: v.]

First, by examining the graph, we can see that [MATH: v_1] is reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

[IMG: /graphics/2bc362fc05ff6eacc279daf1b9f8f8b4]

Next, the vertices [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7] are reachable from [MATH: v_1.] Hence, by transitivity, [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7] are reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

[IMG: /graphics/d069b39690e606c18ab635287850720d]

Finally, the vertex [MATH: v_3] is reachable from [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_7.] Hence, by transitivity, [MATH: v_3] is reachable from [MATH: v_6.]

[IMG: /graphics/4983e79dbcdadc9b152d2ee0ba61b9d8]

No other vertices can be reached. Therefore, the successor set of [MATH: v_6] is [MATH: \{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_7\}.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Transitive Closure and Transitive Reduction

Content:
The transitive closure of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a graph where every possible edge is added while preserving the same reachability relation between vertices as in the original DAG. The transitive closure of a DAG is uniquely determined.

Graphic:

To build the transitive closure, we add a directed edge for every pair of vertices [MATH: v] and [MATH: u] where [MATH: u] is reachable from [MATH: v] indirectly, as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: v_4] is reachable from [MATH: v_1] through the path [MATH: v_1 \to v_6 \to v_5 \to v_4;] hence, we add a new edge [MATH: v_1 \to v_4.]
- [MATH: v_4] is reachable from [MATH: v_6] through the path [MATH: v_6 \to v_5 \to v_4;] hence, we add a new edge [MATH: v_6 \to v_4.]
- No other edges can be added while preserving the same reachability relation.

Content:

Graphic:

The transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a graph where all unnecessary edges are removed while preserving the same reachability relation between vertices as in the original DAG. The transitive reduction of a DAG is uniquely determined.

To build the transitive reduction, we attempt to remove each existing edge while ensuring that all reachability relations of the original DAG are preserved, as follows:

- The edge [MATH: v_1 \to v_5] can be removed because [MATH: v_5] remains reachable from [MATH: v_1] through the path [MATH: v_1 \to v_6 \to v_5.]
- The edge [MATH: v_6 \to v_4] can also be removed because [MATH: v_4] remains reachable from [MATH: v_6] through the path [MATH: v_6 \to v_5 \to v_4.]
